Eli_Asenova/Getty Images Why Rash-Prone Babies Need a Different Diaper Strategy If you’ve changed what feels like 400 diapers today, used enough cream to frost a sheet cake, and the rash is still winning, you’re not doing anything wrong. The good news is that rash-prone skin is super common, and it’s manageable. But (or butt, if you will) diaper rash prevention isn’t just about cream and wipes. The diaper matters too, and the best diapers for diaper rash handle moisture and let skin breathe. Turns out you don’t have to choose.

What Actually Prevents Diaper Rash: The 4 Features That Matter Absorbency: Moisture is the enemy. StatPearls , the NCBI clinical reference, recommends superabsorbent diapers to reduce skin over-hydration. Pampers says Swaddlers use a superabsorbent material that instantly absorbs wetness. Breathability: A 2001 clinical trial in Pediatric Dermatology , conducted by Kimberly-Clark researchers, found that highly breathable diapers reduced severe diaper dermatitis by 38% to 50% compared with standard non-breathable diapers. That includes confirmed Candida (yeast) infections. Breathable diapers for babies help skin stay drier between changes. Fragrance-free and hypoallergenic formulation: StatPearls advises that wipes be free of soap, essential oils, or fragrance, and the same logic makes fragrance-free diapers the smarter pick. “Hypoallergenic” isn’t a regulated term , though, so when shopping for hypoallergenic baby diapers, look for specific testing claims behind the label. Pampers Swaddlers have been fragrance-free in every size since June 2026, and…

items.title: Diapers & Eczema: What Dermatologists Say
items.summary:
Oscar Wong/Getty Images It’s 11 p.m. You’re standing by the crib after changing a diaper, hyper-focused on the glaring rash shining up at you . You’re frantically trying to Google symptoms, causes, and solutions just to soothe your baby’s bottom. Now you've got an arsenal of tabs open and are wondering if this is something you caused.

You didn’t. And for what it's worth, your baby’s butt rash is not a referendum on your parenting. Skin trouble in the diaper area is very common (ugh), but it’s very manageable once you know what you’re dealing with (whew!).

Here’s what you actually need to focus on, minus any panic-inducing packaging jargon.

Is It Diaper Rash or Eczema? All your internet sleuthing raises another question: Is it diaper rash or eczema? Three different things can pop up under a diaper:

Irritant diaper dermatitis (classic diaper rash): Red, sore skin caused by contact with urine, stool, moisture, and rubbing. According to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), it shows up where the diaper touches and usually improves when you remove the irritant. [1] Atopic eczema (atopic dermatitis): A chronic skin-barrier condition, not a contact reaction. The skin doesn’t hold moisture in or keep irritants out as well, so it flares and calms in cycles. Eczema in babies typically starts on the face and scalp, not the diaper area, according to pediatric dermatologist Sarah Stein, MD, for the AAP. [2] Contact allergy (allergic contact dermatitis) : An immune reaction to a specific material, such as a dye, an elastic, or another diaper component. It tends to show up in the…

items.title: Toddlers are not just little people. Their culture deserves respect | Arwa Mahdawi
items.summary:
Small children do not appreciate it when you join in with their singing or throw away their pee-covered leaves. And only a brute would suggest one of them might be tired

Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs.

As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I immediately went down an online rabbit hole and discovered various other people have made similar jokes. items.title: A moment that changed me: at 31 I felt I was running out of time – then my 83-year-old grandma got a tattoo
items.summary:
With my career stalled and my dreams unfulfilled, I was starting to write myself off. But my ideas about ageing were all wrong …

It was the night before my wedding, in the summer of 2024, and I was a couple of months shy of 31. My bridesmaids and I were having drinks with the North American side of my family before the chaos of the big day. In the two years since I’d last seen my grandma Caroline, who lives in Texas and whom I’ve always called Memom, I’d collected a few new tattoos – and I was worried about showing them to her for the first time as her approval means a lot to me.

When Memom saw me, she grabbed my tattooed arm and said: “Let me see.” For a second, I thought she was angry. But to my surprise, she loved them. “These are art!” she said. “Tell me all about them.” I talked her through the abstract fine line piece wrapping around my forearm, and why I’d opted for a filigree dagger in the middle of my upper arm, as well as the significance of the ornamental heart on the back of my right arm.

Continue reading...

I wrote the eulogy to end all eulogies, breaking my own heart with a bottomless well of memories, anecdotes and in-jokes. It was achingly personal and exquisitely her.

  • UK adults: tell us why you think younger people are having less sex

Sex among British adults has slumped in recent decades, with under-45s having half as many monthly encounters as in 1990 and one in three under-25s reporting that they have never had sexual intercourse.

The fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles, or Natsal, found the average adult under 45 now has sex twice a month, continuing a downward trend from four times a month in 1990 and three times a month in 2010.

At the time, Irving, who already had her PhD, was coming back to school for additional training in public health. “We were just like regular girlfriends, passing notes in class and everything,” Rep. Underwood says.

No one wants to talk about it, maybe because there’s still a stigma attached to bathroom issues. Even though I’ve discussed every other postpartum thing under the sun (padsicles! Peri bottles! items.title: So You Think You Have Insomnia. What Now?

Ekaterina Goncharova/Moment/Getty Images When you’re a parent, it’s sometimes hard to tell what is a normal amount of tired and what’s an unhealthy level of exhaustion. Aren’t we all at least a little bit tired all the time? So when should you talk to your doctor about sleep issues? But if you’ve been struggling night after night to fall asleep, you can’t seem to stay asleep, or you never feel well-rested in the mornings , it might be a sign that your sleep needs a little TLC. And yes, even if you’re hesitant to take medications to help you fall and stay asleep , there are actually other treatment options you can try.

Scary Mommy spoke with Dr. Jessica Meers , board-certified sleep psychologist and founder of Rhythm Wellness Sleep Solutions, to find out where you should turn for insomnia help first — and what treatment options even exist.

When should you talk to your doctor about sleep issues? When does “I’m struggling to fall asleep lately” become “I should really see my doctor about this”?

“If it feels like a problem to you, it’s worth having a conversation about,” says Meers. Whether you’re overly tired during the daytime, feel like you can’t sleep long or well enough, or just unhappy with your sleep in one way or another, that’s reason enough to ask for help, she says.

And how do you know if you really have insomnia? Is there a line where sleep troubles become clinical?

items.summary:
In my son’s school district, entering middle school is a rite of passage. Sixth graders go to a new building, get their own locker, and experience freedoms they weren’t allowed in elementary school. 

When my son came home from his first day of middle school, I couldn’t wait to talk about it. “What was the best part of your day?” I eagerly asked. “The food,” he replied.

I wasn’t surprised. Meals are a big deal for a growing boy. But it did make me wonder, what exactly will he eat for lunch every day? 

Long gone are the days when I would pack my son a homemade lunch with a loving note tucked inside. In middle school, he wanted to walk into the cafeteria, review the day’s menu options, stand in line, and buy his lunch. I agreed to the plan because I wanted to support his thirst for independence. But I also hoped I hadn’t unwittingly given him permission to start a junk-food-only diet.

Luckily, there are guidelines schools are required to follow when it comes to serving our kids meals. Those rules aim to make lunchtime enjoyable and healthy for the 30 million students who eat school lunch every day in the United States through the National School Lunch Program (NSLP). Unsurprisingly, they’re a constant work in progress.

What are the School Nutrition Standards? 

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) sets federal requirements for school meals served through the NSLP and the School Breakfast Program. The rules attempt to align school food offerings with nutrition standards outlined in the Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA), the official dietary guidance published by…
items.t: School meals decoded: What’s really on the lunch tray

The research found the average adult under-45 now has sex twice a month, continuing a downward trend from four times a month in 1990 and three times a month in 2010.

items.title: I Travel With A Kid Who Has Severe Allergies. Here Are The Things I Never Thought To Worry About
items.summary:
Anchiy/E+/Getty Images My son has severe allergies, asthma, and celiac disease, so everyday things can sometimes send us to the hospital. And traveling adds another layer of uncertainty. A hotel room that looks clean could be holding fragrances that trigger respiratory symptoms. The swimming pool down the hall could pose problemsThat gluten-free item on the menu during our family night out could be cross-contaminated. As a parent, I’ve learned that keeping my son safe means thinking beyond the obvious risks.

With the colder weather settling in and holiday travel approaching, I knew it was time to take a closer look at what families like mine should be considering before hitting the road or boarding a plane. So, I chatted with experts Dr. Sarah Beebe, a travel advisor and autism travel professional based in Lewes, Delaware, and Dr. Tracy Tyson, a pediatrician with 20 years experience in urgent care, who helped me identify the less obvious triggers families might encounter while traveling—and how to better prepare for them.

The Allergic Kid Through the colder months and when planning trips, I’d always assumed that keeping my son’s inhaler on hand was enough. But a recent hospital stay made me realize his asthma is far more severe than we’d understood, and that I needed to take a more proactive approach to managing it.

I researched all of the common triggers, such as dust, pet dander, pollen, smoke and weather changes. After chatting with Dr. Tyson and Dr. Beebe, I learned of the lesser-known hazards that can lurk in the places we stay and the ways we travel.

items.title: An age gap isn’t always a problem, partner abuse is | Letters
items.summary:
Readers respond to articles on relationships and the age of consent

Regarding Polly Hudson’s article (At 17, I dated a 36-year-old. That decision looks very different to me now, 15 November), I met and lived with a 35-year-old man when I was 17. It is obvious now that the relationship was coercively controlling. A divorced father, he had a need to control every aspect of my life, so no makeup, no northern accent, no fatty food (I became anorexic), no scent, no staying out, no heels, no clothes he didn’t like.

I learned that he had done it all before, pursuing schoolgirls. I tried to break free multiple times, only to find that he had phoned my new partner, or read my diary so he could block my plans. This is about having control, it is not just a sexual preference.

The former heavyweight boxing champion on falling in love at first sight, being diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder, and the much-anticipated match

Born in Manchester in 1988, Tyson Fury – known as the Gypsy King – is a former unified heavyweight world champion. He turned professional in 2008 and in 2015 defeated the long-reigning champion, Wladimir Klitschko, to claim the WBA, IBF, WBO and Ring magazine heavyweight titles. He made a comeback in 2020, and his long-awaited final fight is on 11 December against Anthony Joshua. He appears with his wife, Paris, and seven children in the docuseries At Home With the Furys. A documentary charting his life, Fury, is out on Netflix on 27 November.
